9702-11.1.1.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.1.establish: Most α-particles pass through thin foil almost undeflected because atoms are mostly empty space. Rare large-angle deflections show positive charge and most mass concentrated in a very small nucleus.
9702-11.1.1.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.1.note:
- Most α-particles pass through thin foil almost undeflected because atoms are mostly empty space. Rare large-angle deflections show positive charge and most mass concentrated in a very small nucleus.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.1.self_explain: What does a rare large-angle α deflection show?

9702-11.1.2.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.2.establish: A nuclear atom has a small nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons outside the nucleus in orbitals. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
9702-11.1.2.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.2.note:
- A nuclear atom has a small nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons outside the nucleus in orbitals. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.

9702-11.1.3.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.3.establish: Proton number $Z$ counts protons; nucleon number $A$ counts protons plus neutrons. Neutron number is $A-Z$.
9702-11.1.3.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.3.note:
- Proton number $Z$ counts protons; nucleon number $A$ counts protons plus neutrons. Neutron number is $A-Z$.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.3.self_explain: How is neutron number found from $A$ and $Z$?

9702-11.1.4.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.4.establish: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons; their nucleon numbers differ.
9702-11.1.4.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.4.note:
- Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same proton number but different numbers of neutrons; their nucleon numbers differ.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.

9702-11.1.5.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.5.establish: In ${}^{A}_{Z}X$, $X$ is the element symbol, $A$ is nucleon number and $Z$ is proton number. The nucleus contains $A-Z$ neutrons.
9702-11.1.5.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.5.note:
- In ${}^{A}_{Z}X$, $X$ is the element symbol, $A$ is nucleon number and $Z$ is proton number. The nucleus contains $A-Z$ neutrons.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.5.self_explain: What does the lower number mean?

9702-11.1.6.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.6.establish: In any nuclear process, the total nucleon number and total electric charge are conserved across all reactants and products.
9702-11.1.6.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.6.note:
- In any nuclear process, the total nucleon number and total electric charge are conserved across all reactants and products.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.6.self_explain: Why include every emitted particle when balancing?

9702-11.1.7.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.7.establish: An α-particle is a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons, mass about $4u$, charge $+2e$. β− is an electron and β+ a positron, each mass $m_e$ and charge $-e$ or $+e$. γ is an electromagnetic photon with zero rest mass and zero charge.
9702-11.1.7.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.7.note:
- An α-particle is a helium nucleus: two protons and two neutrons, mass about $4u$, charge $+2e$. β− is an electron and β+ a positron, each mass $m_e$ and charge $-e$ or $+e$. γ is an electromagnetic photon with zero rest mass and zero charge.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.7.self_explain: Compare the masses and charges of β−, β+ and γ.

9702-11.1.8.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.8.establish: An antiparticle has the same mass and opposite electric charge to its particle. The positron is the electron antiparticle: both have mass $m_e$, but their charges are $+e$ and $-e$.
9702-11.1.8.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.8.note:
- An antiparticle has the same mass and opposite electric charge to its particle. The positron is the electron antiparticle: both have mass $m_e$, but their charges are $+e$ and $-e$.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.8.self_explain: What is the antiparticle of an electron?

9702-11.1.9.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.9.establish: β− decay emits an electron and an electron antineutrino; β+ decay emits a positron and an electron neutrino.
9702-11.1.9.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.9.note:
- β− decay emits an electron and an electron antineutrino; β+ decay emits a positron and an electron neutrino.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.9.self_explain: Which neutral particle accompanies β+ decay?

9702-11.1.10.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.10.establish: α-particles from a given nuclear transition have discrete energies. β-particles have a continuous energy range because the available decay energy is shared variably with an emitted (anti)neutrino.
9702-11.1.10.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.10.note:
- α-particles from a given nuclear transition have discrete energies. β-particles have a continuous energy range because the available decay energy is shared variably with an emitted (anti)neutrino.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.10.self_explain: Why do β energies form a continuous range?

9702-11.1.11.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.11.establish: Write nuclides as ${}^{A}_{Z}X$ and balance nucleon number and charge. α emission changes $(A,Z)$ to $(A-4,Z-2)$; β− changes it to $(A,Z+1)$ and emits $e^-$ and $\bar\nu_e$; β+ changes it to $(A,Z-1)$ and emits $e^+$ and $\nu_e$.
9702-11.1.11.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.11.note:
- Write nuclides as ${}^{A}_{Z}X$ and balance nucleon number and charge. α emission changes $(A,Z)$ to $(A-4,Z-2)$; β− changes it to $(A,Z+1)$ and emits $e^-$ and $\bar\nu_e$; β+ changes it to $(A,Z-1)$ and emits $e^+$ and $\nu_e$.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
9702-11.1.11.self_explain: How do β− and β+ change $Z$?

9702-11.1.12.motivate: This idea helps explain observations and solve nuclear questions.
9702-11.1.12.establish: The unified atomic mass unit $u$ is a unit of mass equal to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; $1u=1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
9702-11.1.12.connect: Use this with nuclear notation and conservation to interpret particles and changes.
9702-11.1.12.note:
- The unified atomic mass unit $u$ is a unit of mass equal to one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; $1u=1.66\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.
- Check the particles, numbers and charges carefully.
